newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Topenergy presses Sofia on pipeline concession.
newsitem.headline: Topenergy presses Sofia on pipeline concession.

text.p: Bulgarian-Russian gas joint stock company Topenergy needs a decision from Sofia by February on whether to grant it a concession to transit Russian gas through Bulgaria, Bulgarian newspapers said on Tuesday.

They quoted Topenergy executive director Sasho Donchev as saying Russian gas monopoly RAO Gazprom, which holds 50 percent in the company, was looking at alternative plans including building a gas pipeline under the Black Sea to supply Russian gas to Turkey.
Topenergy officials were not available for comment but have said the Bulgarian government could make a profit of $100 million per year from gas transit through its territory.

Topenergy would need a concession of 30 or 50 years as enlarging the gas transit system on Bulgarian territory is expected to cost some $500 million, and would like a concession covering the whole Bulgarian network.
On Monday, Topenergy invited bids for planning the construction of two transit gas pipeline links to Bulgaria's neighbours Turkey and Serbia and a compressor station.
One of the planned links is a second gas pipeline between the Bulgarian borders with Romania and Turkey. The company needs a plan for the construction of the 270-km link to be ready within two years.
For the last nine years a gas pipeline has linked Bulgaria with Turkey, but Gazprom hopes to boost its exports to Turkey to 30 billion cubic metres from six billion cubic metres.
Topenergy also envisages a 100 km link from Dupnitsa in southwestern Bulgaria to the Serbian border. The plan for the construction of the pipeline should be ready within the first quarter of 1997.

A compressor station for regulating gas volumes will be constructed near the town of Provadia in eastern Bulgaria, which is on the route from the Romanian border to the Turkish border. Its plan should be worked out by the end of the first quarter of 1997.

Bulgaria has potential as a gas distribution centre for the Balkans as it has a 2,200-km pipeline network, including 625 km of transit pipelines which receive and transmit gas from outside the country.

Bulgaria started supplying some gas to Greece in October. Sofia has built a pipeline to Macedonia and is waiting for its western neighbour to complete construction work on its territory and start gas supplies.
